clue.text: Supply pointless gag

indicators.note: without a point: the compass point E (east) is dropped from the word

parts.note: to supply someone is to equip them

explanation.surface: An order to provide a joke that has no point to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointless' takes away E, a compass point, from EQUIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A gag and a quip are both a witty remark or joke.

clue.text: A Spanish female considered as English queen?

parts.note: the Spanish word for 'a' used with a feminine noun is una
mused means thought over, considered

explanation.surface: A Spanish woman is pondered as a candidate for the English throne.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Victoria is famously credited with the line 'We are not amused', so a solver hears her in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase attributed to Queen Victoria, 'We are not amused', makes her the model of someone humourless and displeased.

clue.text: Eccentric peer has French author brought up inside good family

indicators.note: inside means one piece sits within the other
eccentric means odd or out of order, so the letters of peer are rearranged

parts.note: taken as the anagram's letters

indicators.note: in a down answer, brought up means written upward, so the name runs backwards

parts.note: Andre Gide was a French novelist

explanation.surface: An odd aristocrat has a French writer raised in a well-bred household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' suits a down light: the French author's name is written upward, inside the jumbled peer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedigree is a distinguished line of ancestry, the sign of a good family.

clue.text: Member of Gunners team backs ban tackle dire!"

indicators.note: backs here means the word for team goes backwards

parts.note: a mob is a gang or team of people
to bar something is to ban it

indicators.note: tackle means deal with or work on, so the letters of dire are reworked

parts.note: taken as the anagram's letters

explanation.surface: A football supporter's cry that the team should get behind a ban on bad tackles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backs' turns MOB into BOM; 'tackle' rearranges DIRE into DIER. The Gunners suggests Arsenal football club, but here it is the Royal Artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: A bombardier is a junior non-commissioned rank in the Royal Artillery, the gunners of the British Army.

clue.text: Women's semi ending with deep half volley

parts.note: broads is slang for women

indicators.note: ending means the final letter of semi is taken
half means the first half of the word deep is taken

explanation.surface: A women's semi-final ends in a deep half-volley in tennis or cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending' gives I, the last letter of semi; 'half' gives DE, half of deep.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is a simultaneous firing of a ship's guns, a volley of shot.

clue.text: I defend wormhole, cast out in wilderness

indicators.note: cast out means thrown about, so all the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

parts.note: the anagram's letters

explanation.surface: A science-fiction hero vows to guard a wormhole that has been thrown out into the wilds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast out' rearranges all fifteen letters of I DEFEND WORMHOLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A remote isolated place, far from any town, is a wilderness or back of beyond.

clue.text: Monastic leader reduced turn and bum

indicators.note: reduced means cut down, here losing its last three letters

parts.note: about is a turn, as in the military command 'about turn' or an about-face
bot is British slang for the bottom or backside, as is bum

explanation.surface: A head of monks is cut down by turning round and showing his backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' cuts OUT off ABOUT, leaving AB.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbot is the head of an abbey of monks.

clue.text: High-tech period before century or millennium starts

indicators.note: before means the first piece comes ahead of the next

parts.note: a dot is a full stop, or period

indicators.note: starts means the first letters of the following three words are taken

explanation.surface: A date stamp from a hi-tech era just before the century or millennium began.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the dotcom boom of the late 1990s, just before the millennium.
explanation.definitionFit: Dotcom describes internet-based business, the high-tech companies of the online boom.

clue.text: 7A: the first shall be last yet

indicators.note: the first letter is moved to the end of the string

parts.note: read literally, 7A is seven and the letter A

explanation.surface: A biblical quotation, 'the first shall be last', cited from another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is not to another light: 7A is read as SEVEN A, and moving its first letter S to the end gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Even as and yet can both introduce something happening at the same time despite something else, as in 'even as he spoke'.

clue.text: He lets out beginning of laugh, with expression of surprise

indicators.note: beginning of means the opening letter of laugh is taken

parts.note: and means with, together with
Lord! is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A man lets out a chuckle and then an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lets out' looks like laughter escaping, but it means renting property.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord rents out, or lets, property to tenants.

clue.text: Painful, boring thing, endless time spent in school

parts.note: a drill bit is a thing that bores holes

indicators.note: endless means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a school term is a period spent in school

explanation.surface: A pupil describes a dull and painful spell at school that seems never to end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' suggests tedium, but it is a drill. 'endless' drops the M from TERM.
explanation.definitionFit: A bitter experience is painful and hard to accept.

clue.text: Pompous, despicable person captures soldier

indicators.note: captures means one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: turd is a vulgar term for a despicable person
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A scoundrel takes a soldier prisoner and is full of self-importance.
explanation.walkthrough: The vulgar word for a despicable person is standard fare in British cryptics.
explanation.definitionFit: Turgid writing or speech is swollen and bombastic, that is, overblown and self-important.

clue.text: Alight on rocky outcrop -almost all the coast's like this

parts.note: lit means alight, burning
a tor is a rocky peak or outcrop, as on Dartmoor

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the word all itself

explanation.surface: Landing on a rocky crag, nearly all of the shoreline looks like this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last L of ALL. The definition is an adjective: the coast is like this, that is, littoral.
explanation.definitionFit: Littoral means relating to the shore or coastal zone.

clue.text: Pool of water going down below sofa?

parts.note: read as the notes so-fa of tonic sol-fa, the next note going down the scale is me
the second note going down the scale below so and fa is re

explanation.surface: A puddle of water draining away under a settee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sofa' is read as SO and FA, notes of the tonic sol-fa scale (do re me fa so la ti); going down from them gives ME then RE. British usage spells the third note ME, not MI.
explanation.definitionFit: A mere is a lake or pond, a pool of standing water.

clue.text: Tragic heroine's drug-dealing confession?

parts.note: the confession is spoken in the first person, I
sold E: E is slang for the drug ecstasy, so a dealer sold E

explanation.surface: A tragic heroine owns up to dealing drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The confession is the sentence 'I sold E', E being ecstasy. 'heroine's' is 'heroine is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolde is the doomed lover in the Tristan legend and Wagner's opera Tristan und Isolde.

clue.text: Bargain-basement had to cut price ludicrously

indicators.note: ludicrously means absurdly, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: part of the anagram's letters

indicators.note: cut means the word to is shortened by losing its last letter

parts.note: part of the anagram's letters

explanation.surface: A shop had to slash its prices absurdly low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' shortens TO to T; 'ludicrously' rearranges HAD, T and PRICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Bargain-basement and dirt cheap both describe goods sold at very low prices.

clue.text: Petit sac, on dit, du pain?

indicators.note: on dit is French for 'one says', so the made-up word is heard rather than read

parts.note: French for little bag: a small bag would be a bag-ette

explanation.surface: A French question: is a small bag, as people say, a piece of bread?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is in French. A 'little bag' made with the diminutive -ette would be BAGETTE, which sounds like the French loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: Du pain is French for some bread, and a baguette is a long French loaf.

clue.text: Battle of Britain hero ends up getting sack

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means the word is written upward, that is backwards

parts.note: tips are the ends of things
to fire someone is to sack them

explanation.surface: A war hero ends up being dismissed from his job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ends up' looks like the phrase 'finishes by', but 'up' turns TIPS into SPIT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spitfire fighter plane is celebrated as a hero of the 1940 Battle of Britain.

clue.text: More intelligent member of The Wailers?

explanation.definitionFit: Keener means sharper or more acute in mind; a keener is a mourner who keens, that is, wails, for the dead.

clue.text: Holding record as peak location

indicators.note: holding means the second piece is held inside the first

parts.note: an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: Someone holds a record as the location where it peaked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peak location' points to a whole mountain range rather than a single summit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are a European mountain range, a place of high peaks.

clue.text: Artist's short break from conflict?

parts.note: war is armed conflict

indicators.note: short means the word is cut down to its abbreviation, hol

parts.note: a holiday is a break from work

explanation.surface: A soldier's brief leave from the fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts HOLIDAY to HOL, the informal British abbreviation. 'Artist's' is 'Artist is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Andy Warhol was an American pop artist.

clue.text: Poisonous unbeliever rejecting first principle of Christianity

indicators.note: rejecting means a letter is thrown out of the word

parts.note: a sceptic is a doubter, an unbeliever

indicators.note: first principle of means the opening letter of Christianity

explanation.surface: A venomous atheist turns his back on the basic tenet of Christian faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting' removes C, the first letter of Christianity, from SCEPTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Septic means infected with harmful bacteria, so poisonous to the body.

clue.text: Get swag home from it? You'd be lucky!

definitions.text: Get swag home from it? You'd be lucky!

parts.words: Get swag home from it? You'd be lucky!
parts.note: a television contest where lucky contestants take prizes home

explanation.walkthrough: 'swag' looks like a burglar's loot, but here it is the prizes contestants win on television.
explanation.definitionFit: A televised contest where contestants win prizes by luck or skill.

clue.text: Pork has to be a non- starter for Muslim party

parts.note: ham is cured pork

indicators.note: non-starter means the first letter of the word is dropped

explanation.surface: Pork is forbidden, a non-starter for a Muslim political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non-starter' drops H from HAS. The surface plays on pork being forbidden to Muslims.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamas is a Palestinian Islamist political and militant organisation.

clue.text: Beds, perhaps aristocratic?

explanation.walkthrough: Beds is the short form of Bedfordshire, an English county, not furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedfordshire is one example of an English shire; the word is also British slang for upper-class, landed gentry society.

clue.text: Are he and you to hum without vocals? Need a sense of beat

indicators.note: vocals here stands for vowels, the voiced letters, which are all removed from the words

explanation.surface: A music teacher asks two pupils whether they will hum wordlessly, because they need to feel the beat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without vocals' strips the vowels from ARE HE (leaving RH) and YOU TO HUM (leaving YTHM); 'and' just joins them. Vocals look like singing, but they mean vowels.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhythm is the regular pulse in music, which a person with a good feel for timing senses.

clue.text: Using amps and pick Richards stops after first note

parts.note: to elect is to pick or choose

indicators.note: the name Richards stops after its first letter that is a musical note, C, losing everything after it

explanation.surface: Keith Richards picks up an amplified guitar.
explanation.walkthrough: The notes are A to G; the first of them in RICHARDS is C, so it stops there as RIC. The surface suggests a guitar pick and the Rolling Stone Keith Richards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something electric is powered by an electric current, measured in amps.

clue.text: Refuses to deal with humble character who's relatively disliked?

parts.note: to black a business is to boycott it, refusing to deal with it
Uriah Heep is the falsely 'umble' character in Dickens's David Copperfield

explanation.surface: Someone shuns a fawning Dickensian creep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relatively' means among one's relatives: the disgrace of the family.
explanation.definitionFit: A family outcast, the one member the rest disapprove of, is the black sheep.

clue.text: Point and slash with this

parts.note: E is east, a compass point
slash is British slang for urinating, as is pee

explanation.surface: A fencer's weapon, used for thrusting with the point and cutting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slash' looks like a sword cut, but it is British slang for a pee.
explanation.definitionFit: An epee is a fencing sword, a weapon one thrusts the point of.
